• Result: N P T O.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Once the constant shift (here +7) is confirmed using both given example pairs, just add it to each letter's position number for the new word — no need to re-derive the rule for every letter individually.

 

NOTE

 

• Always verify the shift rule against BOTH given example pairs before applying it to the unknown word — a rule that fits only one example may be a coincidence.

question:
Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as are the numbers of the following sets.

(NOTE: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits. E.g. 13 – Operations on 13 such as adding to/subtracting from/multiplying with 13 can be performed. Breaking down 13 into 1 and 3 and then performing mathematical operations on 1 and 3 is not allowed.)

 

(12, 20, 45)

(18, 26, 57)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (13, 21, 47).

 

GIVEN

 

• Example sets: (12, 20, 45) and (18, 26, 57).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Check the relation between the first two numbers (a, b): in (12, 20, 45), b − a = 20 − 12 = 8. In (18, 26, 57), b − a = 26 − 18 = 8. So b = a + 8 in both.

 

• Check the third number: in (12, 20, 45), 2a + 21 = 24 + 21 = 45 ✓. In (18, 26, 57), 2a + 21 = 36 + 21 = 57 ✓. So c = 2a + 21 (equivalently c = a + b + 13).

 

• Test option D (13, 21, 47): b − a = 21 − 13 = 8 ✓; c = 2(13) + 21 = 26 + 21 = 47 ✓. Both conditions hold.

 

• Test the other options: (15,7,19) fails b=a+8; (9,17,29) has b=a+8 but c should be 2(9)+21=39≠29; (11,20,45) fails b=a+8 (20≠19).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Spot the simplest relation first (here, the constant difference b−a = 8), use it to eliminate options quickly, then confirm the surviving option against the second relation (for c).

 

NOTE

 

• When a set has three numbers, always test relations between pairs (a,b), (b,c) and (a,c) systematically — the pattern that repeats identically across both given example sets is the real rule.

question: Satish starts from Point A and drives 47 km towards south. He then takes a right turn, drives 65 km, turns right and drives 65 km. He then takes a right turn and drives 77 km. He takes a final right turn, drives 18 km and stops at Point P. How far (shortest distance) and towards which direction should he drive in order to reach Point A again? (Note: All turns are 90° turns only unless specified.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. 12 km to the west.

 

GIVEN

 

• Start at A, facing south; travel: 47 km south → right → 65 km → right → 65 km → right → 77 km → right → 18 km, stop at P.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Take A = (0,0), north = +y, east = +x. Facing south, each right turn changes facing: south → west → north → east → south.

 

• 47 km south: (0, −47). Turn right (now facing west), 65 km: (−65, −47).

 

• Turn right (now facing north), 65 km: (−65, −47+65) = (−65, 18).

 

• Turn right (now facing east), 77 km: (−65+77, 18) = (12, 18).

 

• Turn right (now facing south), 18 km: (12, 18−18) = P = (12, 0).

 

• Distance from P to A = |12 − 0| = 12 km, and since A(x=0) is to the left of P(x=12), the direction from P to A is west.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Track only net east-west displacement: −65(west) + 77(east) = +12 (net east of A); net north-south: −47+65−18 = 0. So P is 12 km east of A, meaning the return direction from P is 12 km west.

 

NOTE

 

• Facing south, the sequence of right turns cycles south → west → north → east — the opposite cycle of what you get starting from a north-facing direction, so always redetermine the direction cycle for each question.

question: Rakesh ranked 13th from the top and 18th from the bottom in his class. How many students are there in the class?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 30.

 

GIVEN

 

• Rakesh's rank from the top = 13th; rank from the bottom = 18th.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Total students = (rank from top) + (rank from bottom) − 1, since Rakesh himself is counted in both ranks.

 

• Total = 13 + 18 − 1 = 30.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Total = (rank from top + rank from bottom) − 1 is a direct formula — always subtract 1 to avoid double-counting the person himself.

 

NOTE

 

• Forgetting to subtract 1 is the most common mistake in this question type, giving a wrong total of 31 instead of 30.

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

 

Statements:

Some erasers are pens.

Some pens are bags.

 

Conclusions:

(I) Some erasers are bags.

(II) All bags are pens.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Neither conclusion (I) nor (II) follows.

 

GIVEN

 

• Statements: Some erasers are pens. Some pens are bags.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Conclusion I (Some erasers are bags): With two 'Some...are' (I-type) statements sharing a common middle term ('pens'), no definite conclusion connecting 'erasers' and 'bags' can be drawn — the 'some erasers that are pens' and the 'some pens that are bags' need not be the same pens at all. So I does not follow.

 

• Conclusion II (All bags are pens): The statement only says 'some pens are bags', which does NOT mean the reverse ('all bags are pens') — it is a classic conversion error. So II does not follow.

 

• Since neither conclusion is logically guaranteed by the given statements, the answer is 'Neither (I) nor (II) follows'.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Two 'Some A are B' + 'Some B are C' type statements NEVER yield a valid 'Some A are C' conclusion — this is one of the most tested syllogism traps; memorise it to answer instantly.

 

NOTE

 

• Never assume real-world truth or reverse an 'A are B' statement into 'B are A' — syllogism questions must be solved purely on the logical structure given, not on outside knowledge.

question:
Which of the following number will replace the question mark (?) in the given series?

 

1, 2, 6, 15, 31, 56, ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. 92.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 1, 2, 6, 15, 31, 56, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Find the differences between consecutive terms: 2−1=1; 6−2=4; 15−6=9; 31−15=16; 56−31=25.

 

• The differences are perfect squares: 1², 2², 3², 4², 5² = 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.

 

• The next difference should be 6² = 36.

 

• Next term = 56 + 36 = 92.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Whenever consecutive differences look like they are increasing by an odd, growing amount, immediately check if they are perfect squares (1,4,9,16,25,36...) — a very common series pattern.

 

NOTE

 

• Always compute the FULL list of differences before spotting the pattern; stopping after just two or three differences can lead to guessing the wrong rule.

question:
What should come in place of the question mark (?) in the given series?

 

12 28 45 63 ? 102
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. 82.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 12, 28, 45, 63, ?, 102.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Find the differences: 28−12=16; 45−28=17; 63−45=18; so the differences increase by 1 each time: 16, 17, 18, 19, 20...

 

• Next difference (between the 4th and 5th term) = 19: ? = 63 + 19 = 82.

 

• Check: the next difference (between 5th and 6th term) should be 20: 82 + 20 = 102 ✓, which matches the given last term.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• When a series has a known term both before and after the missing one, verify your answer both ways (forward from the previous term, and backward from the next given term) — here both checks confirm 82.

 

NOTE

 

• A series where the differences themselves increase by a constant amount (here, +1 each time) is a second-order arithmetic pattern — always compute at least two consecutive differences to confirm before extending.

question: In a certain code language, 'royal snow blue' is coded as 'tl zw cr' and 'blue two web' is coded as 'rg iq zw'. How is 'blue' coded in the given language?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. zw.

 

GIVEN

 

• 'royal snow blue' → 'tl zw cr'; 'blue two web' → 'rg iq zw'.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Find the word common to both English phrases: 'blue' appears in both.

 

• Find the code common to both coded phrases: 'zw' appears in both 'tl zw cr' and 'rg iq zw'.

 

• Since 'blue' is the only common word and 'zw' is the only common code, blue = zw.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• In this type of coding question, always identify the ONE word repeated across both given phrases first — its code is simply the ONE code repeated across both coded versions.

 

NOTE

 

• This method works only when exactly one word (and one code) is common between the two given phrase-code pairs; if more than one word matches, additional phrases are needed to isolate the exact mapping.

question: Seven boxes, M, N, O, P, Q, R and S, are kept one over the other, but not necessarily in the same order. Only two boxes are kept between M and O. Only N is kept above S. No box is kept below O. R is kept at some place below P but at some place above Q. Which box is kept third above Q?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. P.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 boxes M, N, O, P, Q, R, S stacked; 2 boxes between M and O; only N is above S; no box below O (O is at the bottom); R is below P and above Q.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Number positions 1 (top) to 7 (bottom). 'No box below O' ⇒ O = position 7.

 

• 'Only two boxes between M and O' ⇒ M is 3 positions away from O ⇒ M = position 4.

 

• 'Only N is above S' ⇒ exactly one box (N) is above S ⇒ N = position 1, S = position 2.

 

• Remaining positions {3, 5, 6} are for P, Q, R, with the condition P is above R, which is above Q (i.e., position of P < position of R < position of Q). This gives P = 3, R = 5, Q = 6.

 

• Final stack (top to bottom): N, S, P, M, R, Q, O.

 

• 'Third above Q' means 3 positions above Q's position (6): position 6 − 3 = position 3 = P.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Fix the absolute-position clues first ('no box below O' and 'only N above S') since they pin exact positions immediately, then use the relative clues (M-O gap, P-R-Q order) to fill in the rest.

 

NOTE

 

• 'Third above X' means counting 3 positions upward from X's position, not the 3rd box counting X itself as the first — a frequent off-by-one error.

question: A, B, C, D, E and F are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. E sits second to the left of B. C sits second to the right of F. D is on the immediate left of C. Who is sitting on the immediate right of A?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B.

 

GIVEN

 

• 6 people A-F sit facing the centre. E is second to the left of B; C is second to the right of F; D is immediate left of C.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Number seats 1-6 clockwise (facing centre, clockwise = 'left' direction, counterclockwise = 'right' direction, as all members face inward).

 

• Fix C at seat 1. 'D is immediate left of C' ⇒ D = seat 2. 'C is second to the right of F' ⇒ F = C + 2 (clockwise) = seat 3.

 

• Remaining seats {4, 5, 6} are for A, B, E, with E = B + 2 (second to the left). Testing B = 4 gives E = 6, leaving A = 5 — this is the only assignment that avoids clashing with occupied seats.

 

• Final arrangement (clockwise): seat1=C, seat2=D, seat3=F, seat4=B, seat5=A, seat6=E.

 

• Immediate right of A (seat 5) = one step counterclockwise = seat 4 = B.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Fix one person's seat arbitrarily (here C), derive as many others as possible from the direct clues, and use the process of elimination on remaining seats for the clue involving unassigned people — it avoids testing all 6! arrangements.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the standard convention: when everyone faces the centre of a circular table, moving clockwise corresponds to each person's LEFT, and moving counterclockwise corresponds to each person's RIGHT.

question:
Refer to the following series and answer the question that follows (all numbers are single digit numbers only). Counting to be done from left to right only.

 

(Left) 6 6 4 5 2 2 4 5 1 4 7 7 4 5 9 6 9 2 4 3 8 1 2 8 3 7 1 (Right)

 

How many such odd numbers are there each of which is immediately preceded by an odd number and also immediately followed by an even number?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. 3.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 6 6 4 5 2 2 4 5 1 4 7 7 4 5 9 6 9 2 4 3 8 1 2 8 3 7 1

 

SOLUTION

 

• Number the terms 1 to 27 and scan for an odd digit whose immediate left neighbour is ODD and immediate right neighbour is EVEN.

 

• Position 9 (value 1): left neighbour (position 8) = 5 (odd) ✓; right neighbour (position 10) = 4 (even) ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 12 (value 7): left neighbour (position 11) = 7 (odd) ✓; right neighbour (position 13) = 4 (even) ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 15 (value 9): left neighbour (position 14) = 5 (odd) ✓; right neighbour (position 16) = 6 (even) ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Checking all other odd digits (positions 4, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 22, 25, 26, 27) shows at least one neighbour fails the condition in each case.

 

• Total qualifying: 3.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Underline all odd digits first, then check only those for an odd digit immediately to their left and an even digit immediately to their right — this narrows the scan considerably.

 

NOTE

 

• The order of the condition matters: 'preceded by odd, followed by even' is different from 'preceded by even, followed by odd' — read the exact wording carefully before scanning.

question:
Which of the following letter-number clusters will replace the question mark (?) in the given series to make it logically complete?

 

ZSL 18, VOH 29, RKD 40, NGZ 51, JCV 62, ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. FYR 73.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: ZSL 18, VOH 29, RKD 40, NGZ 51, JCV 62, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Numbers: 18, 29, 40, 51, 62, increasing by 11 each time ⇒ next number = 62 + 11 = 73.

 

• First letters: Z(26), V(22), R(18), N(14), J(10) — each decreasing by 4 ⇒ next = 10 − 4 = 6 = F.

 

• Second letters: S(19), O(15), K(11), G(7), C(3) — each decreasing by 4 ⇒ next = 3 − 4 = −1 → wrap around (add 26) = 25 = Y.

 

• Third letters: L(12), H(8), D(4), Z(26) [since 4−4=0 wraps to 26], V(22) [26−4=22] — each decreasing by 4 (with wraparound) ⇒ next = 22 − 4 = 18 = R.

 

• Combining: FYR 73.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Split the cluster into three independent letter-position sequences (1st, 2nd, 3rd letters) plus the number sequence, and solve each mini-pattern separately — much easier than trying to see all four patterns at once.

 

NOTE

 

• When a letter's position number goes below 1 while subtracting, wrap around by adding 26 (e.g. 4 − 4 = 0 → treat as 26 = Z) — a common trap in decreasing-letter series.

question:
This question is based on the five, three-digit numbers given below.

 

(Left) 515 758 761 726 579 (Right)

 

(Example: 697 – First digit = 6, second digit = 9 and third digit = 7)

(NOTE: All operations to be done from left to right.)

 

What will be the resultant if the second digit of the highest number is added to the second digit of the lowest number?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. 7.

 

GIVEN

 

• Numbers: 515, 758, 761, 726, 579.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Highest number among these = 761; its second digit = 6.

 

• Lowest number among these = 515; its second digit = 1.

 

• Resultant = 6 + 1 = 7.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• First identify the highest and lowest numbers from the whole list before extracting any digits — extracting digits before comparing values is a common source of mistakes.

 

NOTE

 

• In this type of question, 'second digit' always means the tens digit (middle digit) of the 3-digit number, as clarified by the example given (697 → second digit = 9).

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

 

Statements:

Some samosas are burgers.

Some burgers are pizzas.

 

Conclusions:

(I): Some samosas are pizzas.

(II): All pizzas are burgers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Neither conclusion (I) nor (II) follows.

 

GIVEN

 

• Statements: Some samosas are burgers. Some burgers are pizzas.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Conclusion I (Some samosas are pizzas): Two 'Some A are B' + 'Some B are C' statements sharing the middle term 'burgers' do NOT guarantee any relation between 'samosas' and 'pizzas' — the samosas that are burgers need not be the same burgers that are pizzas. So I does not follow.

 

• Conclusion II (All pizzas are burgers): The statement only says 'some burgers are pizzas', which cannot be reversed into 'all pizzas are burgers' — that would be a conversion error. So II does not follow.

 

• Neither conclusion is validly supported by the given statements.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Two consecutive 'Some...are...' statements sharing a common middle term never yield a definite 'Some...are...' conclusion between the two end terms — flag this pattern immediately as 'neither follows' unless additional information is given.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not let real-world plausibility (e.g., 'pizzas being burgers' sounding odd) influence the logic — evaluate strictly on the structure of the statements as instructed.

question: If 1 is added to each even digit and 1 is subtracted from each odd digit in the number 258671543, then what will be the value of middle digit in the new number thus formed?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. 6.

 

GIVEN

 

• Number: 258671543 (9 digits). Rule: even digit → +1; odd digit → −1.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Apply the rule digit by digit: 2(even)→3; 5(odd)→4; 8(even)→9; 6(even)→7; 7(odd)→6; 1(odd)→0; 5(odd)→4; 4(even)→5; 3(odd)→2.

 

• New number: 3 4 9 7 6 0 4 5 2.

 

• With 9 digits, the middle digit is the 5th digit, which is 6.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Since the number has an odd count of digits (9), the middle digit's position is fixed at (9+1)/2 = 5th from either end — apply the even/odd rule to just that one digit (7 → 7−1 = 6) if the full transformation isn't needed elsewhere in the question.

 

NOTE

 

• Apply the addition/subtraction rule to each digit independently based on whether THAT digit is odd or even — do not confuse it with the position (index) of the digit in the number.

question:
Based on the English alphabetical order, three of the following four letter-cluster pairs are alike in a certain way and thus form a group. Which letter-cluster pair DOES NOT belong to that group?

(Note: The odd one out is not based on the number of consonants/vowels or their position in the letter-cluster.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. QA-KG.

 

GIVEN

 

• Pairs: BL-WR, QA-KG, HR-CX, UE-PK.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Convert letters to positions (A=1...Z=26) and find the shift from the first letter to the second, and similarly for the second letters of each cluster.

 

• BL-WR: B(2)→W(23); using a signed (shortest-path) shift, this is −5 (i.e. 5 steps backward: B→A→Z→Y→X→W). L(12)→R(18): +6.

 

• HR-CX: H(8)→C(3): −5. R(18)→X(24): +6.

 

• UE-PK: U(21)→P(16): −5. E(5)→K(11): +6.

 

• QA-KG: Q(17)→K(11): −6 (not −5). A(1)→G(7): +6.

 

• Three pairs (BL-WR, HR-CX, UE-PK) share the pattern (first letter shifts −5, second letter shifts +6); QA-KG breaks this pattern with a −6 shift on its first letter.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Compute the shift for the second letter of each pair first if it looks consistent across all four (here, +6 for all) — then the odd one out must be hiding in the first-letter shift, narrowing your search immediately.

 

NOTE

 

• When counting letter shifts, always check whether going 'forward' or 'backward' around the alphabet gives the shorter, more consistent step — a wraparound (like Z to A) is often involved.

question: In a certain code language, 'dirt is there' is coded as 'mp rc gp' and 'clean the dirt' is coded as 'hk mp bo'. How is 'dirt' coded in the given language?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. mp.

 

GIVEN

 

• 'dirt is there' → 'mp rc gp'; 'clean the dirt' → 'hk mp bo'.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Find the word common to both English phrases: 'dirt' appears in both.

 

• Find the code common to both coded phrases: 'mp' appears in both 'mp rc gp' and 'hk mp bo'.

 

• Since 'dirt' is the only common word and 'mp' is the only common code, dirt = mp.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Identify the single repeated word across both phrases and the single repeated code across both coded strings — they must correspond to each other.

 

NOTE

 

• This shortcut works cleanly here because exactly one word (and exactly one code) is shared between the two phrase-code pairs.

question:
In a certain code language,

P + Q means 'P is the father of Q',

P # Q means 'P is the mother of Q',

P & Q means 'P is the wife of Q',

and P % Q means 'P is the sister of Q'.

 

How is V related to D if 'V % L & C + B % D'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Mother's sister.

 

GIVEN

 

• Code: '+' = father of, '#' = mother of, '&' = wife of, '%' = sister of. Expression: V % L & C + B % D.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Break the expression into its parts: V % L → V is the sister of L. L & C → L is the wife of C. C + B → C is the father of B. B % D → B is the sister of D.

 

• Since C is B's father and L is C's wife, L is B's mother — and since B and D are siblings (B is sister of D), L is also D's mother.

 

• Since V is L's sister, and L is D's mother, V is D's mother's sister, i.e. D's maternal aunt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Decode the expression piece by piece from left to right, building a small family tree as you go (L=wife of C=mother of B,D; V=sister of L) — trying to hold the whole chain in your head at once is error-prone.

 

NOTE

 

• 'P & Q means P is wife of Q' tells you Q is the husband — carefully track whose spouse is whose to correctly infer parentage of the children in the family.

question: Seven people B, C, D, I, J, K, and L are sitting around a circular table facing the centre of the table. Only three people sit between D and L, when counted from the right of L. Only three people sit between K and I, when counted from the left of K. B sits to the immediate right of D. J is an immediate neighbour of L as well as I. Who sits second to the left of C?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. J.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 people around a circular table facing centre: 3 people between D and L (counted from L's right); 3 people between K and I (counted from K's left); B is immediate right of D; J is an immediate neighbour of both L and I.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Number seats 0-6 clockwise (clockwise = 'left', counterclockwise = 'right', since all face the centre). Fix L = 0.

 

• 'Three people between D and L, counted from the right of L' ⇒ moving counterclockwise (right) 4 steps from L reaches D ⇒ D = seat 3.

 

• 'B is immediate right of D' ⇒ B = seat 2 (one step counterclockwise from D).

 

• 'Three people between K and I, counted from the left of K' ⇒ I is 4 steps clockwise from K, i.e. I = K + 4 (mod 7). Testing available seats {1,4,5,6} for K gives a valid, clash-free solution only at K = 1, I = 5.

 

• Remaining seats {4, 6} are for J and C. 'J is an immediate neighbour of both L(0) and I(5)': neighbours of seat 0 are {6, 1}; neighbours of seat 5 are {4, 6}; the common seat is 6, so J = 6, leaving C = 4.

 

• Final arrangement (clockwise): 0=L, 1=K, 2=B, 3=D, 4=C, 5=I, 6=J.

 

• 'Second to the left of C' (seat 4): move 2 steps clockwise (left) ⇒ seat 4+2 = 6 = J.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Resolve the two 'X people between... counted from a direction' clues into exact seat numbers first (these fully fix D and I relative to L and K), then use the neighbour clue for J to pin down the last two people by elimination.

 

NOTE

 

• 'Counted from the right/left of X' specifies the DIRECTION of counting, not just how many people are between two individuals — get the direction wrong and the whole arrangement mirrors incorrectly.

question:
What should come in place of the question mark (?) in the given series based on the English alphabetical order?

 

BMV, EOT, HQR, KSP, ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. NUN.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: BMV, EOT, HQR, KSP, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• First letters: B(2), E(5), H(8), K(11) — each +3 ⇒ next = 11 + 3 = 14 = N.

 

• Second letters: M(13), O(15), Q(17), S(19) — each +2 ⇒ next = 19 + 2 = 21 = U.

 

• Third letters: V(22), T(20), R(18), P(16) — each −2 ⇒ next = 16 − 2 = 14 = N.

 

• Combining: N U N.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Split a 3-letter cluster series into three independent single-letter series (1st letters, 2nd letters, 3rd letters) and solve each with simple constant differences — much faster than trying to see the whole cluster's pattern at once.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch for series where different letter-positions move in DIFFERENT directions (here the third letter decreases while the first two increase) — don't assume all three columns follow the same direction.

question:
In the following triads, each group of letters is related to the subsequent one following a certain logic. Select from the given options, the one which follows the same logic.

RAMP - PRMA - RPAM

SEND - DSNE - SDEN
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. QUAD - DQAU - QDUA.

 

GIVEN

 

• Pattern: RAMP → PRMA → RPAM, and SEND → DSNE → SDEN.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Label positions 1,2,3,4. From RAMP(R,A,M,P) to PRMA(P,R,M,A): new1=old4, new2=old1, new3=old3, new4=old2. Verify with SEND(S,E,N,D)→DSNE: new1=old4(D), new2=old1(S), new3=old3(N), new4=old2(E) = D,S,N,E = 'DSNE' ✓.

 

• From PRMA(P,R,M,A) to RPAM(R,P,A,M): this is simply swapping adjacent pairs — new1=old2, new2=old1, new3=old4, new4=old3. Verify with DSNE(D,S,N,E)→SDEN: new1=old2(S), new2=old1(D), new3=old4(E), new4=old3(N) = S,D,E,N = 'SDEN' ✓.

 

• Apply both steps to QUAD (Q,U,A,D): Step 1 (new1=old4,new2=old1,new3=old3,new4=old2) → D,Q,A,U = 'DQAU' — matches the option's middle term.

 

• Step 2 (swap adjacent pairs) on DQAU(D,Q,A,U) → Q,D,U,A = 'QDUA' — matches the option's third term exactly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Derive the exact letter-position permutation from the FIRST given example, confirm it with the SECOND example, then mechanically apply that same permutation to each option's first word and check both resulting words — this avoids guessing by 'look and feel'.

 

NOTE

 

• These triad questions almost always use a fixed positional permutation (not a alphabetical shift); write out each word by position number (1,2,3,4) to spot the exact pattern precisely.

question:
What should come in place of the question mark (?) in the given series?

 

18, 22, 30, 42, 58, ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. 78.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 18, 22, 30, 42, 58, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Find the differences: 22−18=4; 30−22=8; 42−30=12; 58−42=16.

 

• The differences increase by 4 each time: 4, 8, 12, 16, so the next difference = 16 + 4 = 20.

 

• Next term = 58 + 20 = 78.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Differences increasing by a constant amount (here +4 every step) signal a second-order arithmetic series — just extend the difference sequence by one more step and add it to the last term.

 

NOTE

question:

question: Six people, A, B, C, D, E and F, are sitting in a row, facing north. A sits to the immediate left of B. C sits third to the left of B. D is an immediate neighbour of B. F sits to the immediate right of C. D sits to the immediate left of E. Who sits at the extreme right end of the line?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. E.

 

GIVEN

 

• 6 people in a row facing north (positions 1 to 6, left to right). A is immediate left of B; C is third to the left of B; D is an immediate neighbour of B; F is immediate right of C; D is immediate left of E.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Let B's position = p. Then A = p−1 (immediate left of B), and C = p−3 (third to the left of B).

 

• 'D is an immediate neighbour of B' means D = p−1 or p+1. Since p−1 is already A's seat, D = p+1.

 

• 'D is immediate left of E' ⇒ E = D+1 = p+2.

 

• 'F is immediate right of C' ⇒ F = C+1 = p−2.

 

• So positions relative to B: C=p−3, F=p−2, A=p−1, B=p, D=p+1, E=p+2 — six consecutive seats, so p−3 ≥ 1 and p+2 ≤ 6, giving p = 4.

 

• Final seating (left to right): C(1), F(2), A(3), B(4), D(5), E(6).

 

• The extreme right end (position 6) is occupied by E.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Express every person's position relative to a single reference person (here B) using simple +/− offsets; once all six offsets are known, the valid range for B's own position is usually forced to a single value, as it was here (p=4).

 

NOTE

 

• All six positions must lie between 1 and 6 with no gaps or repeats — using this constraint to pin down the reference person's position is faster than trial-and-error placement.

question: If 1 is added to each even digit and 2 is subtracted from each odd digit in the number 54286379, how many digits will appear more than once in the new number thus formed?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Three.

 

GIVEN

 

• Number: 54286379 (8 digits). Rule: even digit → +1; odd digit → −2.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Apply the rule digit by digit: 5(odd)→3; 4(even)→5; 2(even)→3; 8(even)→9; 6(even)→7; 3(odd)→1; 7(odd)→5; 9(odd)→7.

 

• New number digits: 3, 5, 3, 9, 7, 1, 5, 7.

 

• Count frequency of each digit: 3 appears twice (positions 1,3); 5 appears twice (positions 2,7); 9 appears once; 7 appears twice (positions 5,8); 1 appears once.

 

• Digits appearing more than once: 3, 5, 7 — that is 3 digits.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• After transforming all digits, simply tally each resulting digit's frequency in a quick frequency table — count how many DISTINCT digit-values repeat, not how many extra occurrences there are.

 

NOTE

 

• The question asks how many digits appear MORE THAN ONCE (i.e. distinct repeated values), not the total count of repeated occurrences — read carefully to avoid answering a different question.

question:
In the following triad, each group of letters is related to the subsequent one following a certain logic. Select from the given options, the one which follows the same logic.

DIVE - DEVI - EVID

BEAR - BRAE - RAEB
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. COLD - CDLO - DLOC.

 

GIVEN

 

• Pattern: DIVE → DEVI → EVID, and BEAR → BRAE → RAEB.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Label positions 1,2,3,4. From DIVE(D,I,V,E) to DEVI(D,E,V,I): position 1 and 3 stay the same (D, V); positions 2 and 4 are swapped (I↔E). So the rule is swap letters at positions 2 and 4.

 

• Verify with BEAR(B,E,A,R)→BRAE: swap positions 2&4 (E↔R) gives B,R,A,E = 'BRAE' ✓.

 

• From DEVI(D,E,V,I) to EVID(E,V,I,D): this is simply a left-rotation by one position (each letter shifts one place left, and the first letter wraps to the end): D,E,V,I → E,V,I,D ✓.

 

• Verify with BRAE(B,R,A,E)→RAEB: left-rotation by one gives R,A,E,B = 'RAEB' ✓.

 

• Apply both steps to COLD (C,O,L,D): swap positions 2&4 (O↔D) gives C,D,L,O = 'CDLO' — matches the option's middle term.

 

• Left-rotate CDLO(C,D,L,O) by one: D,L,O,C = 'DLOC' — matches the option's third term exactly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Derive the transformation rule from the FIRST given example (here: swap 2nd & 4th letters, then rotate left by one), confirm it against the SECOND example, and apply mechanically to the options rather than guessing by pattern-matching letters visually.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish between a 'swap of specific positions' and a 'rotation of the whole word' — mixing these two operations up is the most common error in this question type.

question: India submitted its 4th Biennial Update Report to the UNFCCC in December 2024. What is the full form of UNFCCC?
option_1: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
option_2: Union Network for Future Climate Control
option_3: United Nations Forum for Climate Coordination
option_4: United Nations Foundation for Climate Cooperation
solution_text:
The correct answer is United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• UNFCCC stands for the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, an international environmental treaty adopted at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992 and entered into force in 1994. (UNFCCC — संयुक्त राष्ट्र जलवायु परिवर्तन ढांचा सम्मेलन)

 

• India submitted its 4th Biennial Update Report (BUR-4) to the UNFCCC in December 2024, reporting on its greenhouse gas emissions inventory, mitigation actions, and progress towards its climate commitments.

 

• The UNFCCC provides the overarching international framework under which subsequent climate agreements, such as the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015), were negotiated.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option A.

 

Additional Information

 

• The UNFCCC's supreme decision-making body is the Conference of the Parties (COP), which meets annually — e.g. COP28 in Dubai (2023) and COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan (2024).

 

• India ratified the Paris Agreement in 2016 and has committed to targets like achieving net-zero emissions by 2070, announced by PM Narendra Modi at COP26 in Glasgow (2021).

 

• India's climate commitments also include reducing the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030 (from 2005 levels) and achieving 50% cumulative electric power installed capacity from non-fossil fuel sources by 2030.

 

NOTE

 

• Union Network for Future Climate Control (Option B), United Nations Forum for Climate Coordination (Option C), United Nations Foundation for Climate Cooperation (Option D): These are all incorrect/fabricated expansions; the correct and only official name is the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.

question: In 2025, which authority raised serious objections to the Aparajita Bill 2024, calling its proposed punishments under BNS excessively harsh and disproportionate?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Central Government.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In 2025, the Central Government raised objections to West Bengal's Aparajita Woman and Child (West Bengal Criminal Laws Amendment) Bill, 2024, calling some of its proposed punishments under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) framework excessively harsh and disproportionate. • The Aparajita Bill was passed by the West Bengal Legislative Assembly in the aftermath of public outrage over crimes against women, proposing enhanced punishments, including the death penalty, for certain offences like rape.

 

• Since criminal law falls under the Concurrent List of the Indian Constitution, such state amendments require the President's assent (given after Union Government review) before they can become law — this is the context in which the Centre's objections arose.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option D.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 is the new criminal code that replaced the colonial-era Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860, effective from 1 July 2024.

 

• The other two new criminal law codes that replaced older laws are the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) (replacing the CrPC) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) (replacing the Evidence Act).

 

• State amendments to central criminal laws are a recurring point of Centre-State friction, since uniformity in criminal law across India is a key constitutional concern.

 

NOTE

 

• National Commission for Women (Option A): A statutory body that advocates for women's rights and typically supports, rather than objects to, stronger punishment for crimes against women.

 

• Law Commission of India (Option B): An advisory body on legal reform, not the authority that raised this specific objection.

 

• Supreme Court (Option C): The apex judiciary; while it can rule on constitutional validity if challenged, the objection described here (during the assent process) came from the Central Government.

question: Which of the following was the impact of the Election Commission of India Network (ECINET) on the publication of Index Cards during elections?

option_2: Publication was delayed by several additional weeks.

Additional Information

• Continuous digitisation of the electoral process is part of the ECI's broader push towards greater transparency, speed and voter convenience in Indian elections.

• Delayed by weeks (Option B): Contrary to the actual impact, which was to speed up, not delay, the availability of these records.

question: What percentage did CPI inflation touch in April 2025 in India, marking a near six-year low?

• This decline was largely driven by a sharp fall in food inflation, particularly softer prices of vegetables and other perishables, alongside a favourable high base effect from the previous year.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.

 

Additional Information

• WPI (Wholesale Price Index), in contrast, measures price changes at the wholesale/producer level and is released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

 

• Lower inflation generally gives the RBI room to cut the repo rate, supporting economic growth by making borrowing cheaper for businesses and consumers.

question: The Mussalman Wakf (Repeal) Bill, 2025, seeks to remove the outdated Mussalman Wakf Act of ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1923.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Mussalman Wakf (Repeal) Bill, 2025, seeks to repeal the outdated Mussalman Wakf Act, 1923, a colonial-era law that has been rendered largely redundant by subsequent, more comprehensive wakf legislation. (मुसलमान वक्फ अधिनियम, 1923 — निरसन विधेयक)

 

• The Mussalman Wakf Act, 1923 was originally enacted to provide for the compulsory publication of accounts of wakf (Islamic charitable/religious endowments) by their managers (mutawallis).

 

• This 1923 Act was superseded in practical effect by later, more detailed legislation — the Wakf Act, 1954 and subsequently the Wakf Act, 1995 — making the older Act obsolete and a candidate for formal repeal as part of legislative clean-up.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option B.

 

Additional Information

 

• A 'wakf' is a permanent dedication of movable or immovable property by a Muslim for purposes recognised as religious, pious or charitable under Islamic law.

 

• The Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025 was a separate, significant piece of legislation passed in 2025 that made substantial changes to the management and administration of wakf properties in India, distinct from this specific repeal of the old 1923 Act.

 

• Periodic repeal of obsolete laws is part of the Government of India's ongoing exercise to remove outdated and redundant legislation from the statute books.

 

NOTE

 

• 1953, 1943 and 1933 (Options A, C, D): None of these correspond to the actual year of the original Mussalman Wakf Act being repealed; the correct year is 1923.
